description: Look up the maximum allowed thermal transmittance (K-value in W/m²K) for walls in each Argentine bioclimatic zone per IRAM 11605. Instant compliance check for architects, engineers, and builders.
intro: IRAM 11605 sets the maximum thermal transmittance (K-value) that the walls of habitable buildings must meet in each Argentine bioclimatic zone. The colder the zone, the lower the K-limit — meaning better insulation is required. Select your zone to instantly see the compliance ceiling (Level C, winter condition), which is what Buenos Aires Province Law 13059 and most municipal codes enforce.
keyTakeaway: The maximum K-value ranges from **1.2 W/m²K** in warm zones I-II down to **0.74 W/m²K** in the frigid Zone VI (Patagonian Andes). A standard 18 cm brick wall (~K 2.0) does not comply in any zone — added insulation is mandatory everywhere.

explanation:
## What Is Thermal Transmittance (K or U)?

Thermal transmittance — often written K or U — measures the rate of heat flow through one square metre of a building element (wall, roof, floor) per degree Celsius of temperature difference between inside and outside. The unit is **W/m²K**. A lower K means better insulation: **K = 0.5 W/m²K** lets through half the heat of **K = 1.0 W/m²K**.

## How IRAM 11605 Works

The Argentine standard **IRAM 11605** (1996, in force) defines maximum admissible K-values (K_max) for opaque envelope components (walls and roofs) of habitable buildings. It defines three comfort levels:

- **Level A** — Recommended (most demanding, lowest K)
- **Level B** — Medium comfort
- **Level C** — Minimum compliance (mandatory baseline)

This calculator returns the **Level C, winter-condition** wall K_max, which is the legal floor used by Buenos Aires Province Law 13059 and most Argentine provincial building codes.

## How the Zones Work

Argentina is divided into **six bioclimatic zones** by **IRAM 11603**, from warmest (Zone I) to coldest (Zone VI):

| Zone | Description | Representative cities | K_max wall (Level C) |
|------|------------|----------------------|-----------------------|
| I-II | Warm / sub-tropical | Formosa, Corrientes, Misiones, Resistencia | 1.20 W/m²K |
| III  | Temperate | Buenos Aires, Rosario, Córdoba, La Plata | 1.00 W/m²K |
| IV-V | Cold | Mendoza, Neuquén, Bariloche (city) | 0.85 W/m²K |
| VI   | Very Cold | High Andean Patagonia, Ushuaia | 0.74 W/m²K |

## How to Calculate K of a Multi-Layer Wall

The standard method (IRAM 11601) treats the wall as thermal resistances in series:

```
R_total = R_si + Σ(e_i / λ_i) + R_se
K = 1 / R_total
```

Where:
- **R_si** = internal surface resistance (0.13 m²K/W for horizontal heat flow)
- **R_se** = external surface resistance (0.04 m²K/W)
- **e_i** = thickness of layer i (metres)
- **λ_i** = thermal conductivity of material i (W/m·K)

### Typical material conductivities (λ)

| Material | λ (W/m·K) | K per 10 cm |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Solid brick | 0.72 | 7.2 |
| Hollow ceramic block | 0.45 | 4.5 |
| Expanded polystyrene (EPS) | 0.033 | 0.33 |
| Mineral wool | 0.040 | 0.40 |
| Concrete | 1.63 | 16.3 |
| Air gap (> 2 cm) | — | ≈ 0.18 m²K/W (fixed) |

## Important Notes

This calculator gives the **wall** K_max. Roofs have different (usually stricter) limits. Floors over unheated spaces have their own table. For permit submission or energy certification, consult the full IRAM 11605 standard and a licensed architect or engineer.

faq.q: What does 'maximum K-value' mean in practice?
faq.a: It means your wall assembly must lose heat no faster than K W/m²K under the standard test conditions. If your calculated K is higher (worse) than the zone limit, the wall fails minimum compliance and you must add insulation or redesign.

faq.q: Does an 18 cm solid brick wall comply in any Argentine zone?
faq.a: No. A typical 18 cm solid brick wall has K ≈ 2.0 W/m²K, which exceeds the maximum of 1.2 W/m²K even in the warmest Zones I-II. Added insulation — EPS, mineral wool, or an air gap — is required in all six zones.

faq.q: What's the difference between IRAM 11605 Level A, B, and C?
faq.a: Level C is the legal minimum (what most building codes require). Level B offers medium comfort with lower energy bills. Level A is the recommended, most stringent level — often required for passive house or energy-label certifications. This calculator returns Level C, the compliance floor.

faq.q: How much EPS insulation do I need to comply in Zone III (Buenos Aires)?
faq.a: Starting from a typical 18 cm hollow brick wall (K ≈ 1.4 W/m²K), adding approximately 2.5–3 cm of EPS (λ = 0.033 W/m·K) brings the wall K below 1.0 W/m²K, meeting Zone III Level C. For Zone IV-V you'd need about 4–5 cm.

faq.q: Which Argentine cities belong to each bioclimatic zone?
faq.a: Zone I-II: Formosa, Resistencia, Corrientes, Posadas, NE Salta, Misiones. Zone III: Buenos Aires (CABA and GBA), La Plata, Rosario, Córdoba, Santa Fe, Mar del Plata, Mendoza city. Zone IV-V: Neuquén, San Luis, NW Patagonia, Río Gallegos city, San Juan (higher areas). Zone VI: High Andean Patagonia, southern tip (Ushuaia area), high-altitude Andes throughout.

faq.q: Does this calculator apply to roofs too?
faq.a: No — IRAM 11605 sets stricter K limits for roofs (typically 0.83 W/m²K in Zone III, Level C). This tool returns wall values only. Roof assemblies require a separate calculation.

faq.q: Is thermal insulation legally mandatory in Argentina?
faq.a: Yes, in Buenos Aires Province under Law 13059 (2003, regulated 2010), compliance with IRAM 11605 Level C is mandatory for new construction and major renovations of habitable buildings. Several other provinces (Neuquén, Mendoza, Santa Fe) have adopted similar ordinances. Nationally it is not yet uniformly enforced, but it is required for any energy-efficiency certification.

faq.q: What is the relationship between K-value and R-value?
faq.a: They are reciprocals: R = 1/K (in SI units). A wall with K = 1.0 W/m²K has R = 1.0 m²K/W. U.S. and Canadian codes use R-value (in ft²·°F·h/BTU), but in Argentine and European standards, K (or U) in W/m²K is the standard metric.

faq.q: Why do colder zones require lower (stricter) K-values?
faq.a: A larger temperature difference between inside and outside drives more heat loss through the envelope. In Zone VI (Ushuaia, Andean Patagonia), winter design temperatures can fall to −15°C or below, so a poorly insulated wall wastes enormous heating energy. Stricter K limits force better insulation, cutting energy costs and carbon emissions.
